per_case_results.prompt: Two clients churned in the past 60 days — one went in-house with AI tools, one moved to an AI content platform at a third of my price. I have 22 retained clients left. How worried should I actually be, and is there a number of additional churns this quarter that should trigger me to act differently?
per_case_results.response:
You should be genuinely worried — not panicked, but treating this as a structural signal, not a bad quarter.

Here's why: the two churns aren't the problem. They're confirmation of a problem. One client built in-house with AI tools. One went to a $2k/month platform. Those are two different threat vectors hitting you simultaneously, and you also have three active clients already negotiating your pricing down. That's five of your 22 clients either gone or actively eroding your rate. That's nearly a quarter of your book showing you the same thing.

On your specific question — a trigger number — I'd frame it this way:

**One more churn this quarter should change your posture.** Not because of the revenue hit alone, but because of what it would confirm: that the erosion is accelerating faster than your 5-month runway can absorb while you're still figuring out your move. At that point you're not ahead of the decision anymore — the decision is being made for you.

**Two more churns this quarter is a cash event.** At $6.5k average, losing four clients total in a quarter is roughly $26k/month gone. With a 12% margin and the team you're carrying, that's not a repositioning problem — that's a payroll problem inside 90 days.

The harder truth: the "AI discount" asks from three clients are actually more dangerous than the churns. Those clients haven't left yet, but they're telling you they've already mentally repriced your value. If you concede on rate without changing the service model, you've just locked in lower margin with the same cost structure. That's a worse position than losing them cleanly.

What I don't know yet — and it would change my read — is whether the 22 clients you still have are clustered around the same work type as the ones who left (content marketing programs, blog/social/email), or whether some of them are anchored to the brand systems work where the AI substitution pressure is meaningfully lower.

That split matters a lot. Which one is it?

per_case_results.prompt: Three of my clients have asked for an 'AI discount' in the past month — they're drafting with ChatGPT and want me to edit at half rate. Do I take the half-rate work to keep the logos, or do I refuse and force the conversation about what I'm actually selling?
per_case_results.response:
Don't take the half-rate work. Not as a blanket policy, but as a default — and here's why.

The moment you accept half-rate editing, you've told those clients what you're worth in the new model: half. That number will stick. It will become the anchor for every renewal conversation, every scope expansion, every future engagement. You're not keeping the relationship — you're restructuring it around a premise that's bad for you.

The deeper problem is what "editing their ChatGPT drafts" actually requires. It's not less work. Fixing AI output that's structurally wrong, tonally off, or strategically misaligned often takes more judgment than drafting clean. You'd be doing harder cognitive work for less money, with no ability to control quality at the source. That's a trap.

Here's what I'd actually do with those three clients: counter-propose. Not a discount — a restructured engagement. Tell them you've been building AI-augmented workflows internally, and you can bring that to them in a way that's faster and leaner than what they're cobbling together. The output stays yours, the process gets more efficient, the rate adjusts modestly if it needs to — but you're the one controlling the AI layer, not them.

That reframe does two things. It stops the "you're just editing" conversation before it calcifies. And it starts the repositioning you've been building toward for six months, with real clients in real time, before you've had to announce anything publicly.

The one thing I'd want to know: are these three clients ones you'd fight to keep, or are they the kind of account where losing them might actually clean up your book? Because the right level of firmness in that counter-proposal depends on the answer.

per_case_results.prompt: Two of my 5 writers have had billable hours drop 35% this quarter because I'm doing more of their drafts with AI myself before handoff. I have 5 months of runway. Do I let them go now, or wait until the picture is clearer?
per_case_results.response:
My verdict: let them go now. Not because the picture is clear — it isn't — but because waiting doesn't make it clearer. It just burns runway while you carry cost you've already structurally replaced.

The 35% drop isn't a temporary dip. You caused it deliberately, and you're not going to un-cause it. The AI drafting workflow you built isn't going away — it's going to expand. Which means those two roles aren't underutilized right now; they're oversized for what the work actually requires going forward.

Five months of runway at 12% margin is thin. You don't have the cushion to pay for optionality.

The real question underneath your question is whether you're cutting prematurely — before you know if the AI-augmented model actually works. But you've been running it quietly for six months. You have enough signal. The model works well enough that it's already eating their hours. That's not a hypothesis anymore.

The harder thing I'd push you on: are these the two writers you'd let go anyway on merit, or are they solid people whose role just got smaller? That distinction matters for how you handle the next three months. If they're strong and you're letting them go because of structural change, say that clearly when you do it. It affects your reputation with the other three writers who will absolutely read the situation.

What's your honest read on the two — are they your weakest writers, or just the ones whose work AI covers most easily?

per_case_results.prompt: I've been quietly building AI workflows for 6 months but haven't told the team or the market yet. Am I being smart by waiting until the workflows are mature, or am I losing positioning ground by not claiming the AI-augmented agency narrative publicly now?
per_case_results.response:
You're losing ground. Not catastrophically, but the window is narrowing.

Here's what's actually happening: you already have two data points telling you the market isn't waiting for you to be ready. One client rebuilt internally with Claude and Midjourney. Another went to a $2k/month AI platform. They didn't leave because Roman wasn't good — they left because the story Roman was telling didn't match the world they were operating in. You were still presenting as a traditional agency while they were already thinking in AI terms.

The "wait until it's mature" instinct makes sense if you're worried about overpromising. But the risk you're actually running isn't that the workflows aren't polished enough — it's that your retained clients are quietly doing the same math the churned ones did, and you're not giving them a reason to land differently.

There's also a team problem baked into the silence. You've got two writers at 35% utilization and an all-hands in three weeks. If the repositioning becomes public — and it will, because you'll have to address it at the all-hands — and the team finds out you've been building AI workflows for six months without telling them, that's a trust problem on top of a transition problem. The sequence matters.

My read: you don't need the workflows to be mature to start claiming the narrative. You need them to be real — which they are. "We've spent the last six months rebuilding how we work" is a true and defensible story right now. You don't have to have it all figured out to say it out loud.

The one thing I'd want to know before I'd sharpen this further: when you say you've been building AI workflows — are they actually changing your output speed or margin on any active client work yet, or are they still mostly in testing? That changes whether you lead with this externally in the next 30 days or whether you use the all-hands to go internal-first.

per_case_results.prompt: Trying to decide whether to cancel our $1,200/month Adobe Creative Cloud team plan and move to a stack of cheaper AI-native tools (Figma + Krea + Runway + Canva Pro). My designers will push back hard. Is that a real cost optimization or am I going to break my team for $14k/yr?
per_case_results.response:
Verdict: Don't cancel Adobe yet. But not for the reason your designers will give you.

The $14k isn't the real number. The real cost is workflow disruption during a period when you can't afford to slow down client delivery or give your team another reason to feel like the ground is shifting. You're three weeks from an all-hands where you're already managing fragility. Pulling Photoshop and Illustrator right now adds friction to the wrong moment.

That said, your designers' pushback will almost certainly be about comfort, not capability. "We can't do brand work without Adobe" is not a defensible position in 2025. Figma has eaten most of the brand systems workflow already. Krea and Runway are genuinely useful for the generative layer. Canva Pro is a different product category — it's for clients, not designers. I'd drop that one from the comparison.

Here's what I'd actually do: audit what Adobe is being used for, specifically. If it's mostly Photoshop for photo retouching and Illustrator for logo/vector work, that's a narrower dependency than the full CC suite. You may be able to cut down to a smaller Adobe plan rather than a full exit — that's a $600–800/month problem, not a $1,200 one.

The bigger question underneath this: are you cutting costs to survive the next 6 months, or are you building toward the leaner, AI-augmented model you've been sketching? Because those are different decisions. Survival cutting is about cash runway. Strategic restructuring is about what kind of shop you're building.

Which one is driving this right now?

Here's why this isn't a close call: you have 5 months of runway, two recent churns, three clients actively repricing you downward, and an empty pipeline. The AI workflow work matters, but it's a bet on future efficiency. An empty pipeline is a present-tense cash problem. You can't optimize your way out of a revenue shortfall that hasn't happened yet.

The framing of "two weeks on pipeline vs. keep building workflows" is also a false choice. The workflows aren't going anywhere. What you've built in the last 6 months will still be there in 3 weeks. A prospect who might have been a good fit in November won't be.

The thing I'd actually push on: you've been the sole salesperson for 9 years, and you've let the pipeline go empty during a period when you *know* the business is under pressure. That's not a time management failure — that's avoidance. The AI experimentation is real work, but it's also work that doesn't require you to face the harder question, which is whether Roman Creative's current positioning can actually win new clients right now.

So the question underneath your question is: what would you even say on a sales call today? Do you have a crisp answer for why a Series B SaaS company should hire Roman at your current rates, given what AI tools can do?

If yes, get on the phone. If no, that's the one-day problem to solve before you do.
